title: The Balusters by David Lindsay-Abaire on Broadway #thebalusters #manh...
transcript: From David Lindsay-Abaire, book writer of Kimberly Akimbo, comes The Balusters, a scalding commentary on social dynamics with a side of micro-aggressions and elitism. Shortly after settling into a picturesque, historically-protected neighborhood, newcomer Kyra Marshall finds that the homeowners association meetings are anything but a walk in the park. Initially, a dispute surfaces over how to handle a dangerous intersection lacking any signage or signals. As tensions rise and Kyra identifies longstanding problematic aspects of the association and its leadership, things escalate way beyond just arguing over a stop sign. Some players are definitely more culpable than others, but no one is fully safe. Hypocrisy is rampant, with everyone quick to assume the worst in others while exempting themselves from their own well-intentioned but offensive behaviors. The zippy pacing and delightful performances make this one a likely crowd-pleaser despite the jokes being a little too on the nose and the messaging being severely heavy-handed. The way the play develops is also not perfect, becoming less realistic and more cartoonish, and the overall focus waning — but I was laughing enough that this didn't really bother me. More than the way it integrates social issues did I enjoy how it humorously illustrates our propensity toward petty drama. Above all else, I enjoyed how childish and petulant the characters became — some people really just need to be listened to and have a thirst for importance, even when they have nothing valuable to say. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
classificationReason: Creator shares first-hand opinion on the Broadway production — praises pacing and performances, critiques heavy-handed messaging and cartoonish escalation, notes personal laughter. Clear review of the stage production.
